clue.text: B-Bunthorne's first clue b-blitzed by Araucaria's first two - could be a Messerschmitt?

indicators.note: the first of a name is its opening letter, here repeated by the stammer the setter writes in
something blitzed is bombed to bits, so these letters are blown apart and land in a new order
the first two of the setter's name are its opening pair of letters

blocks.note: Bunthorne is a fellow setter; his first letter, stammered as printed, comes twice
taken as written
the stammer before blitzed supplies one more letter
Araucaria is another setter; his name opens with these two letters

explanation.surface: A stammering tribute to two famous crossword setters, ending with a question about a German aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The stammered letters are not decoration: every B counts in the anagram. Messerschmitt made fighter planes in the war, but after it built a tiny three-wheeled bubble car.
explanation.definitionFit: The Messerschmitt KR200 was a small postwar microcar with a domed perspex canopy, the classic example of this kind of vehicle.

clue.text: Stinker of a problem by setter for "Petty Officer"

blocks.note: BO, body odour, is a smelly personal problem
the sun sets every evening, so it is a setter

explanation.surface: A puzzle setter has produced a nasty problem with the answer Petty Officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the compiler talking about himself, but it is the thing that sets in the west.
explanation.definitionFit: A bosun, or boatswain, is a ship's officer in charge of equipment and crew, ranked as a petty officer in navies.

clue.text: House of correction for regressive little boy, last resort

indicators.note: regressive means going backwards, so the name is read from its end
to re-sort is to sort again, putting the letters into a fresh order

blocks.note: Rob is a short form of the boy's name Robert
taken as written

explanation.surface: A house of correction as the last resort for a boy who keeps sliding back into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last resort' reads as a set phrase, but resort is split off as a signal to re-sort the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A borstal was a British detention institution for young offenders, a place meant to reform them.

clue.text: Appearing dishevelled, hangdog role attacked with such a sarcastic comment

indicators.note: something dishevelled is untidy and messed up, so the following words are jumbled

blocks.note: the four words supply every letter

explanation.surface: Someone looking a mess and sheepish is greeted with a sneering remark.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration counts a second word, which the grid does not give: the phrase borrows WHAT, the first word of 21-across, so the anagram makes the full saying while the lights hold the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mocking greeting for someone arriving scruffy or bedraggled, a typical example of a sarcastic remark.

clue.text: Name the place, so to speak

indicators.note: 'so to speak' tells us to go by how a word is said rather than spelt

blocks.note: a site is a place or location

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to identify the location.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite is to mention or quote someone as an authority, the verb sense of naming them.

clue.text: Within dilapidated realm, Shed appears so?

definitions.text: Within dilapidated realm, Shed appears so?

indicators.note: 'Within' places one word inside the letters of another
something dilapidated has fallen apart, so the word that follows is rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
a shack is a crude hut or shed

explanation.surface: A shed in a run-down kingdom looks the part.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a hut in a dilapidated setting appears tumbledown.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramshackle describes a building so badly kept that it looks close to collapse, as a neglected shed would.

clue.text: Contrarily entered the bar?

indicators.note: contrarily means the other way round, so the two halves of the phrase swap places

blocks.note: to have entered is to have got in

explanation.surface: Someone walked into the pub, against expectation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bar' looks like the pub someone went into; it is a bar of metal.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingot is a block of cast metal such as gold, often called a bar of bullion.

clue.text: Commercial for the River Test

blocks.note: the Indus is a great river of Pakistan
a trial is a test

explanation.surface: An advert for the River Test, a famous English trout stream.
explanation.walkthrough: The Test is a chalk river in Hampshire famous for fly fishing, so 'River Test' looks like one name; it is two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial relates to trade and manufacturing, close in sense to commercial business activity.

clue.text: Beast's depressing call when eagle's head and leonine tail removed

indicators.note: a word's head is its opening letter
a word's tail is its closing letter
removed tells us the selected letters are taken out of the rest

blocks.note: grey can mean dull and gloomy
to phone is to call
opening letter, removed from the first word
closing letter, removed from the second word

explanation.surface: A mythical beast cries mournfully after losing the eagle's head and lion's tail that make it what it is.
explanation.walkthrough: Eagle's head and lion's body are exactly what a griffin has, which makes the deletions look like zoology.
explanation.definitionFit: The gryphon, or griffin, is a legendary creature with an eagle's head and wings on a lion's body.

clue.text: Having forced Euro entry, one can compete no longer

indicators.note: something forced is pushed out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A team that forced its way into a European competition still cannot take part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' marks the word as archaic: tourneys belong to the Middle Ages.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourneyer was a knight who fought in medieval tournaments, a contest that has long since vanished.

clue.text: See 21
Mad? They must be cracked!

blocks.note: first meaning: crazy, informally
second meaning: hard-shelled fruits opened by cracking

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' also means crazy, so the second half seems to restate the first; it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for insane and also the plural of hard-shelled kernels that need breaking open to eat.

clue.text: See 21
Smuggling scam established to circumvent prohibition

indicators.note: to circumvent is literally to go around, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: a con is a swindle
trad is short for traditional, long established
a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: A smuggling racket set up to get round the law.
explanation.definitionFit: Contraband means trade in forbidden goods, that is smuggling, as well as the goods themselves.

clue.text: Excitable type of crow with bolt, perhaps, swallowed

indicators.note: 'perhaps' suggests a possible version of the word, so its letters may be rearranged
something swallowed ends up inside another, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: the hooded crow is a grey-and-black European crow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A highly strung kind of crow has gulped down something, perhaps a bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot-blooded means passionate and quick-tempered, easily stirred to strong feeling.

clue.text: Scrappy 0-0, ie zilch, of very little order

indicators.note: scrappy means disorganised and in bits, so the letters are put together afresh

blocks.note: each nought is read as the letter it resembles
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scrappy goalless draw, nothing at all, of very little sporting order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' sounds like ranking in a table; it is the biological order, and 'very little' describes its microscopic members.
explanation.definitionFit: Heliozoic relates to the Heliozoa, sun animalcules, an order of tiny single-celled protozoa.

clue.text: Game that's bound to stop

blocks.note: to bound is to jump or hop
to scotch a plan is to put a stop to it

explanation.surface: A sports fixture that is certain to be called off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to'; bound is really a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopscotch is a children's playground pastime of hopping through squares chalked on the ground.

clue.text: Drink's first dispatched, then aroused

indicators.note: the first letter is sent away, so the word loses its opening

blocks.note: brandy is a drink

explanation.surface: A first drink is knocked back and then someone gets amorous.
explanation.definitionFit: Randy is British slang for sexually excited, lustful and keen.

clue.text: Conductor of mass in church, perhaps?

definitions.text: Conductor of mass in church, perhaps?

blocks.note: surface reading: a priest leading a service
setter's reading: one who steers a heavy body, such as a ship, through its course

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' and 'church' point at a priest; mass is weight, and the conductor is a guide steering something heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot guides ships through harbours or flies aircraft, so steers and leads a large moving object.

clue.text: Stand for left and centre, but not right

indicators.note: something not right is wrong or out of place, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political stance of left and centre, but not right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But not right' looks like an instruction to drop the R for right; no letter goes, and 'not right' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is a sloping reading desk for a speaker, a type of stand for books or notes.

clue.text: Songwriter provides occasion for dancer and a prancer

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dance
taken as written
Prancer is one of Santa's reindeer, and deer prance

explanation.surface: A songwriter lays on a dance for someone who moves elegantly and another who struts.
explanation.walkthrough: Dancer and Prancer are both names of Santa's reindeer, a hidden joke behind the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A balladeer composes or performs ballads, narrative songs, so is a kind of songsmith.

clue.text: Tasmanian pet should be chained, as devilish

indicators.note: devilish behaviour is wild and wicked, so the letters run riot into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice that a pet in Tasmania be kept chained up, because it behaves like a devil.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tasmanian devil is a famous fierce marsupial, which makes 'devilish' look like the animal itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The echidna, a spiny egg-laying mammal, lives in Tasmania; calling it a pet is a playful stretch.

clue.text: Bird's mate approaching ducks

blocks.note: cock is old British slang for a pal, as in 'wotcha, cock'
at as in 'at the door', arriving close
a duck in cricket is a score of nought, and two noughts look like these letters

explanation.surface: A bird's partner is heading towards some ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' and 'ducks' sound like birds; both are slang, and a duck is a batsman's zero score in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: The cockatoo is a crested parrot from Australia and nearby islands, a kind of bird.

clue.text: Hear wife's homily to sot that couldn't order, as "last orders" was hours ago

annotation.answer: WHAT SORT OF TIME DO YOU CALL THIS THEN

definitions.text: Hear wife's homily to sot that couldn't order, as "last orders" was hours ago

indicators.note: to order is to put in a sequence, so the preceding words are arranged afresh

blocks.clueFragment: Hear wife's homily to sot that couldn't
blocks.note: all seven words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A wife lectures her drunken husband stumbling home long after the pub has shut.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines the answer: it is the very rebuke the wife delivers. 'Last orders' is the British pub's final call for drinks before closing.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the stock indignant question for someone arriving home very late, here the drinker rolling in after closing time.

clue.text: Tango dancing in Polynesia?

definitions.note: names a place found there rather than a noun; the question mark marks the definition by location

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and settle into new positions

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Doing an Argentine dance on a South Pacific island.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonga is a kingdom made up of islands in the South Pacific, part of the Polynesian region.

clue.text: See 21
Asian city of fragrancy

indicators.note: 'of' here means made out of, so the letters come from inside the next word

blocks.note: the run of letters sits inside this word

explanation.surface: An Asian city known for its sweet smells.
explanation.definitionFit: Agra is a city in northern India, home of the Taj Mahal, so an Asian urban centre.

clue.text: See 3
Hard, 1 down? To a point

definitions.note: a phrase meaning sharpened, standing for the past participle

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
the numeral written out
D is the abbreviation for down in crossword grids

explanation.surface: A crossword solver, stuck on a hard clue, gets there in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 down' looks like a cross-reference to another clue; it is just the number and the direction spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Honed means sharpened on a whetstone, so brought to a fine edge or tip.

clue.text: Bittersweet drama reviewed "without a clue", almost withdrawn

indicators.note: to review a play is to look it over again, here reworking its letters
'without' in the old sense of outside, so one part wraps around the other
almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
withdrawn means drawn back, so those letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bittersweet play gets reviews calling it clueless and is nearly pulled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bittersweet' looks like a critic's adjective for the drama; it is the plant's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dulcamara is the botanical name for woody nightshade, a climbing plant commonly called bittersweet.
